title: BM25 and lexical search
summary: A ranking function that scores documents by term overlap with the query, weighted by how rare each term is and normalised for document length.
what: BM25 scores a passage by how often the query's terms appear in it, discounting terms that appear everywhere and correcting for the fact that longer passages contain more of everything by chance.
why: Exact terms matter. Identifiers, statute numbers, defined contract terms and product names must match literally, and an embedding model will happily rank a paraphrase above the exact string you asked for.
how: Each term contributes idf x saturated term frequency. The saturation means the tenth occurrence of a word adds far less than the second, and the length normalisation prevents long documents winning on volume alone.
in_this_project: Implemented by hand in harness/golden/bm25.py rather than pulled from a library, because it is used to pool judgment candidates for the golden set and that scoring has to be auditable. Postings are stored in array('i') rather than lists of tuples: 51,310 chunks produce roughly 15 million postings, and the tuple form costs gigabytes of object overhead for no benefit. Index build takes about 5 seconds.

formula.notation:
score(q,d) = sum over terms t in q of
  idf(t) * ( tf(t,d) * (k1+1) ) / ( tf(t,d) + k1 * (1 - b + b * |d|/avgdl) )

idf(t) = log( 1 + (N - df(t) + 0.5) / (df(t) + 0.5) )

terms.meaning: how often term t appears in passage d
how many passages contain t at all
this passage's length against the average
term-frequency saturation; higher means repetition keeps counting
length normalisation strength; 0 disables it entirely

advantages: No training, no model, no GPU
Exact identifiers and rare terms rank correctly
Scores are explainable term by term
limitations: No notion of meaning: a paraphrase scores zero
Vocabulary mismatch between query and document is fatal
Stopword and tokenisation choices quietly change results

pitfalls: Comparing BM25 scores across queries — they are not calibrated and have no fixed range
Assuming a high score means relevance rather than term overlap

use: Identifiers, codes, names and defined terms
As one half of a hybrid retriever
avoid: Alone, when users ask in their own words
